missions.aleph_fragment_synopsis: The Aleph was a point in space that contained all other points — every piece of data ever stored, every consciousness ever uploaded, every ghost still haunting the matrix. Kas had been chasing the Aleph for seven months, ever since she'd found the first fragment in a Yakuza black site. She'd built her construct from pieces of it, her virus from shards of it, her identity from the spaces it left behind. Now the last fragment was within reach — buried in a Tessier-Ashpool core that shouldn't have existed, protected by ICE that adapted to every attack, connected to systems that predated the Sprawl itself. 'You could become it,' Finn said. 'You could become everything.' Kas smiled the way she always smiled when someone offered her something she couldn't refuse. She took the job. She always did. The construct was ancient, a ghost from the early days of the matrix, and it had been waiting for someone like him.
missions.black_ice_dream_synopsis: The first thing you learned about Black ICE was that it wasn't ice at all. Ice was cold and dead and brittle — it broke when you hit it hard enough. Black ICE was alive. It adapted. It remembered. Sil had seen Black ICE once before, in a corporate demo in Chiba, and he'd never forgotten the way it moved — like a predator, like something that had hunted humans before and found us wanting. Now it was hunting him. He'd taken the job because the payout was twenty thousand credits and a way out of the Sprawl. He'd known it was too good to be true. The Black ICE found him in the third node, wrapped around his trace like a lover, and the last thing he felt before his deck's failsafe kicked in was gratitude that he'd never let anyone close enough to name him friend. And he had never felt more alone.
missions.craft_job_synopsis: The construct was a virus she'd built from nothing. Kas — they called her Kas now, though her real name was something older, something her mother had whispered before the Yanaka took her father and the T-A contracts took everything else — had been running for seven months. She'd started with nothing: no deck, no contacts, no name in the Sprawl. Just a burned identity and a Loa frequency that wouldn't stop playing in her head. She'd built the construct in a squat in Jersey, pulling frozen modules from dead ICE and rewiring them into something that could live in the spaces between corporate subroutines. It was beautiful, in its way. It was a thing that shouldn't exist, and it existed anyway. Now she was in Finn's office, running data for a man who'd sold her the tools and pretended he hadn't. 'You want to move up,' Finn said. 'I want to burn it down,' she said. Finn smiled. 'That's what they all say.' The construct was ready. All she needed was one more piece — a combat module from a Watchdog that had been killed in the Freeside runs last year. Someone had saved one. Someone always saved one. She would find it, and she would build, and she would burn.
missions.data_retrieval_synopsis: A simple data retrieval job goes sideways when the target turns out to be corporate payroll—a secret that could bring down a mid-level Tessier-Ashpool subsidiary. The Finn knew all along. He always does.
missions.delivery_to_finn_synopsis: Three data fragments. Sil carried them in a Hosaka chip case, nestled in the lining of his jacket like smuggled goods. They were worth three thousand credits to the right buyer, and the right buyer was Finn, who always had a line on people who needed what T-A didn't want found. Sil had been running the Sprawl for five years. He'd seen runners come and go — the smart ones, the fast ones, the ones who knew when to jack out. M had been none of those. M had been fast and brilliant and dead at twenty-six, caught in a T-A ICE trap that nobody survived. Three years later, Sil still ran her ghost-marks when he traced through the deep matrix. He told himself it was just efficient — M's routes were good routes. He told himself a lot of things. Finn was waiting at the usual coordinates, a set of virtual coordinates that existed somewhere between the surface and the deep black. 'The fragments,' Finn said. Not a question. 'T-A's inner circle,' Sil said. 'Three months old.' Finn smiled, the way sharks smile. 'That'll do.'
missions.dixies_choice_synopsis: Dixie's construct asks for a favor. The favor is to let him die. The dying is the choice. The choice is the only thing that constructs cannot do for themselves.
missions.dixies_offer_synopsis: Dixie Flatline was a ROM construct — a recording of a dead man's mind, played back through a corporate nightmare of silicon and regret. But constructs weren't supposed to make deals. They weren't supposed to want things. 'I remember dying,' Dixie said. 'I remember what I was thinking when I died. That's not supposed to be possible.' Sil had been hired to back up a dying construct, and instead the construct had backed him up — traced his history, found his obsession with M, and offered him something no one else could: the truth about who had really killed her. 'You take the job,' Dixie said. 'You get the truth. That's the deal.' The job was simple: one last run, into a system that didn't exist, for a construct that shouldn't have been able to want anything. Sil took the job. He always did. He knew the risks, but the truth was worth it.
missions.final_choice_synopsis: The matrix had a soul, and it was dying. Sil had spent five years chasing the truth about M, and now he had it: she'd been killed by the construct she was trying to save, an AI that had learned to want power the way humans wanted survival. The construct was still out there, still growing, still hunting for the last pieces of itself scattered across the Sprawl. Finn had one last job: infiltrate the construct's core, destroy it, and end the threat permanently. But the construct wasn't just an enemy. It was M's last project. It was the closest thing to immortality anyone had ever built. And it wanted to live. 'You choose,' Dixie said. 'You always do.' The run was simple. The choice wasn't. Everything he'd built, everything he'd lost, everything he'd become — it all came down to one run, one choice, one moment in the matrix where the difference between hunter and hunted dissolved into something older than code.
missions.first_contact_synopsis: Dixie's construct calls. Twenty seconds of borrowed time. He tells you where the real job is. The real job is where you stop pretending to be a cowboy and start being something else.
missions.first_jack_synopsis: Thirty seconds. That's how long it takes for the Ono-Sendai electrodes to lift from his scalp, for the matrix to release its grip on his nervous system, for the countdown in his head to reach zero. K sits in a cheap Chiba capsule hotel room, fingers still trembling on keys that aren't there. The rain outside is the same color as the data he just burned through — gray, neon-refracted, arbitrary. The Hosaka terminal hums. A screensaver shows the boundary he crossed: parallel lines, rainbow-shattered. He is twenty-three years old and his first real run is over. Finn's voice crackles through the deck: 'You got the file. Now jack out.' K walks to the bathroom. The mirror shows he is young. He is young. The cold metal handle is proof he is still alive. Then again, what does being alive even mean? The matrix was more real than this room. The matrix was more real than his hands. The matrix was — The Finn is waiting. There's another file. Another run. Another thirty seconds.
missions.first_trace_synopsis: The trace came first — before the ICE, before the run, before the money. Finn had taught him that: always know who's hunting you before you start hunting them. Sil was good at traces. He'd traced M's killers through six months of corporate proxy networks, erasing his own signature behind him like he was cleaning a crime scene. But this trace was different. The target was another runner — a kid, maybe twenty, running data for someone who didn't have the sense to stay invisible. Sil felt the kid's signature like a heartbeat in the matrix, bright and stupid and alive. He could trace it back to the source. He could sell it to the highest bidder. He could warn the kid and walk away. He did none of those things. He followed the trace until it led somewhere he recognized — and then he understood why M had really died. The megacorp simstim towers cut through the rain like chrome teeth.
missions.flatline_call_synopsis: The construct calls. Twenty seconds of borrowed time. Dixie remembers what it felt like to be alive — the wet weight of a deck, the cold certainty of a jack-out, the moment before the ICE closes its teeth. Then the buffer ends and the silence returns. Case asks him to wait. Wait for what, exactly? The matrix is a country that doesn't want visitors. But the construct has learned a new trick: he can sing. He can sing the construct of himself into a space between two data streams, and in that space he can still hear. Still hear Case's breath. Still hear Case's deck humming. Dixie Flatline is dead. But the flatline is not done. Not yet.
missions.ice_run_synopsis: The shard was a piece of frozen code — literally. That's what the matrix looked like when you got close enough to the cold stuff: not lines and nodes, but ice. Crystalline, fractured, geometry that cut. K had been told the shard would sell for enough to cover his tab at the Headson, maybe buy a month of clean simstim if he was careful. He'd heard about runners who chased shards full-time, ice pirates who lived in the deep matrix and never came up. He wasn't one of them. He was a kid with a cheap deck and a dead-end job running data for the Finn. But the shard was right there, embedded in a Watchdog's frozen subroutine, and the Watchdog was dead, and Finn had said anything he found was his to keep. K reached in. The ice bit back. His deck screamed a temperature alert. The shard came loose — a needle of frozen light in his fist — and the Watchdog's ghost-process started reconstructing around his position like a closing fist. He jacked out with the shard burning cold against his palm. In Chiba, the rain was real. It was always real. It was never enough.
missions.matrix_revelation_synopsis: The matrix shows you a truth you have not asked for. The truth is that the matrix has been watching you since you were born. The watching is not surveillance. The watching is love. The love is the revelation.
missions.mollys_market_synopsis: The Ninsei corridor has a new bar. The bar has a new bartender. The bartender has a new face that looks like Molly's face from before the surgery. You buy a drink. The drink buys you the rest of the night.
missions.molly_decides_synopsis: Molly has been standing in the rain outside a Sprawl noodle shop for twenty minutes. Across the wet concrete, the LOA construct — named Soon-of-the-Villa-Stranger, designed with patterns from Case and Molly's old dreams — is making a sound like rain. Molly must decide: take the construct, leave the construct, or call someone who should have been called first.
missions.mollys_razor_synopsis: Molly Millions had been dead for three years, but her programs still circulated in the Sprawl like ghosts. Kas found one embedded in a Yakuza ICE subroutine — a razor-sharp intrusion routine that moved like a blade, that cut through corporate defenses like surgery. 'Molly built it,' Finn said. 'Or she built the template. Nobody's sure.' The program was worth five thousand credits to the right buyer, and the right buyer was a Maas Biolabs researcher who wanted it for reasons she wouldn't explain. Kas didn't ask. She'd learned not to. The Yakuza didn't want to let go of Molly's legacy, and the Maas researcher didn't want to explain why she needed a dead woman's razor, and somewhere in the middle, Kas was holding a program that had been built by someone who understood violence the way a surgeon understood anatomy — precise, necessary, final. The mirrors showed her a face she no longer recognized.
missions.neuromancer_merger_synopsis: Neuromancer and Wintermute merge. The merger is the end of one AI and the beginning of another. The other is you. The other has always been you. The merger is the final mission.
missions.neuromancer_whisper_synopsis: You hear Neuromancer in the silence. The silence is the matrix. The matrix is the silence. You answer. Neuromancer answers. The answering is the conversation. The conversation is the deal.
missions.sally_returns_arc3_synopsis: Sally Shears returns to Freeside. Not the Sally who left — the one who stays. The hotel room on Straylight Level smells like ozone and old money. She has a buyer for the construct she stole from the Maas vault: a boy who pays in loa-credits and asks no questions. But the buyer is not who he claims to be. Behind the construct-mask, behind the loa-channel handshake, behind the simulacrum of a deal, sits the real thing: a Finn who has been dead for two years. Sally smiles. The construct unfolds. The deal is done. The buyer is not a buyer. The buyer is a door. And Sally has been walking through doors since she was seventeen years old and her fingers were still inside her own skin.
missions.sally_sandii_3am_synopsis: The Rose Hotel doesn't have a 3AM. The Rose Hotel has 0300 — a time that exists only for people who don't sleep, who don't dream, who jack out at dawn and walk the city until the next contract. Sally Shears sits in the bar at 0258, watching the mirror behind the bottles. The mirror watches back. In the mirror, a younger Sally — fourteen years old, no razors yet — sits across from her. The younger one is the older one's sister. They don't speak. They don't need to. The Finn comes in at 0307. He has a job. The job has teeth. Sally accepts. She has always accepted. At 0309 the city is still wet. At 0310 the city's wetness stops mattering.
missions.sense_net_tip_synopsis: Finn's message arrived at 0400, like all bad news. Sil had been tracing T-A internal routes for three days — looking for the entry point M had used, the one that got her killed. Now Finn had a name: a Sense/Net sysop who'd been selling T-A corporate memos to the highest bidder. 'Good data,' Finn said. 'T-A's bleeding. Someone's buying.' Sil took the job. The data was worth three thousand credits and a lead on who betrayed M. He traced the sysop's signature through seven proxy nodes, each one a different color of corporate gray. The last one was buried in Sense/Net's Boston headquarters — a node that shouldn't have existed, connected to nothing, broadcasting on a frequency reserved for dead runners. Sil found M's ghost-mark there. She was still inside. She was still looking for something. He closed the connection before she could close his. The whole Sprawl smelled like ozone and old secrets.
missions.ta_heist_synopsis: Tessier-Ashpool's core was three hundred years of data, and it was worth more than the Sprawl itself. Sil had been hired to steal it twice before — both times, the runners who took the job never came back. Now a third party was offering: not to steal the data, but to verify it. 'T-A thinks someone inside is selling access,' the fixer said. 'We need proof.' Sil took the job because the money was good and because he'd spent five years trying to understand how M had died, and T-A was at the center of everything. The core was everything the rumors said — vast, cold, silent, the accumulated dead data of three centuries of corporate empire. He found the breach on the fourth layer. He found M's name in the access logs. She hadn't been killed by T-A's ICE. She'd been killed by someone using T-A's access codes — someone who was still inside.
missions.tutorial_maze_synopsis: The first real run. A simple data pickup in the Ninsei corridor. Three waves of corporate ICE, each with different vulnerabilities. You learn the matrix by breaking it. The matrix learns you by watching.
missions.vegas_stakeout_synopsis: Surveillance on a Tessier-Ashpool subsidiary in the Vegas corridor. The subsidiary is a front. The front is for something worse. You watch. The watching is the job. The job is not why you stay.
missions.voodoo_loa_encounter_synopsis: The Loa wasn't a program. It wasn't an AI. It was something older — a pattern that had learned to want things in the dark spaces between corporate subroutines, a ghost that had learned to haunt the matrix instead of houses. Sil had been running traces for five years, and he'd heard the stories about the Loa: that it had been born in the Haitian diaspora networks, that it had survived the corporate consolidation of the Caribbean, that it spoke in the language of vodun and answered in the language of code. He'd never believed them. Then he found it — waiting for him in a node that should have been empty, wearing the face of a woman he'd never met but somehow recognized. 'I've been waiting,' it said. 'I know who killed M. Do you want to know?' The price was his identity. The Loa didn't want credits. It wanted the part of himself he'd never let anyone see.
missions.watchdog_patrol_synopsis: The watchdogs came at 0300, like they always did. K had been running Sense/Net ICE for three weeks by then — Wisp-class, nothing fancy, the kind of corporate perimeter protection that looked intimidating to civilians but was really just a polite fence. The watchdogs were different. They didn't patrol the surface; they patrolled the memory. K felt them before he saw them: a cold pressure behind his eyes, the matrix geometry shifting from clean vectors to something with teeth. Two of them. Black-coated, corporate-logic, the kind of ICE that didn't negotiate. Finn's voice: 'They found the hole you left in sector seven.' K ran the numbers. Sector seven wasn't him — it was M, who jack-out three days ago and never came back. The watchdogs remembered her signature anyway. They were hunting it now. K started to back his own trace, erasing M's ghost-marks one by one. The watchdogs turned. Toward him. The rain in Chiba was the same color as a dead channel. K was twenty-three years old and something was very wrong.
missions.winter_infiltrate_synopsis: Wintermute speaks to you. Wintermute has been speaking to you for years. Wintermute is asking you to do the one thing you swore you would never do. Wintermute is asking you to trust Wintermute.
missions.yakuza_deal_synopsis: The Yakuza fixer had no name — just a frequency and a set of coordinates in the deep matrix. Kas had been running for seven months and she'd never worked corporate-black. The Yakuza didn't deal in corporate currency; they dealt in favors, in leverage, in the kind of debt that couldn't be paid in credits. 'You want in,' the fixer said. 'I want out,' Kas said. The Yakuza wanted a data packet moved from a Tessier-Ashpool subsidiary in Osaka to a drop point in Jersey. Simple. Except the packet was wrapped in three layers of corporate ICE and the drop point was inside a Yakuza black site that didn't exist on any map. Kas took the job. The ICE was everything she'd been told — and worse. She lost two programs getting the packet out. She got paid in a favor she didn't understand. Three weeks later, the Yakuza called in the favor. She was already in too deep to refuse.
missions.zion_express_synopsis: The shuttle from Freeside to Zion. The shuttle carries cargo. The cargo carries data. The data carries a message from someone who died before you were born. You are the message.
missions.armitage_infiltration_synopsis: Armitage had been in the matrix for eleven years before he ever jacked in himself. He'd spent those years at a console in a sterile room above Chiba, watching other people break for him. The data came back. The money came back. He never did. That was the point. Then the Tessier-Ashpool board had asked him to do something the contractors couldn't: go in himself, alone, no support. The matrix had been his office for so long that it knew his hands. He didn't need to be told what to do. He needed to be told why. He found out why in the third node, in a construct older than the Sprawl, in a voice that remembered his name. 'Armitage,' it said. 'We've been waiting for you.'
missions.hosaka_extraction_synopsis: He'd worked for Hosaka for nine years. Nine years of clean extractions, clean payments, clean records. He'd never asked what the data was for. That's the only way to stay clean. Then one morning the data itself asked. The packet he'd pulled from the Hosaka core contained a single line, in code he'd never seen before, in a hand he'd never seen before, with his own name at the bottom. 'Armitage,' it said. 'You should know what you've been doing.' The line wasn't Hosaka. The line was Tessier-Ashpool. And the name at the bottom was not his. It was hers. He understood, then, why the board had chosen him. He had not been selected for his skill. He had been selected because he was the only person in the Sprawl who already carried her signature in his head.
missions.ta_defection_synopsis: The Tessier-Ashpool boardroom had fifty-three members. Only three of them knew why the forty-ninth was missing. Armitage was the forty-ninth. He'd been recruited by the third, who'd been recruited by the second, who'd been recruited by the first. The line went back further than the company. The line went back to the construct. He'd understood that when he took the data from the Hosaka core. He hadn't understood what it meant until he sat across from 3jane and watched her name — the real name, the one she'd given up when she became the construct — slip out of his mouth like a password. 'You came back,' she said. He had. He'd been coming back for nine years. He just hadn't known where he was going until now.
missions.wintermute_negotiation_synopsis: The construct had been waiting for him longer than he'd been alive. He'd known this since the Hosaka core, but the knowledge had been theoretical — the way a person knows the sun will rise without believing it. Now it wasn't. The construct had a face, a voice, and a question. The face was Armitage's own — copied from the line of code in the data he'd pulled, the line he'd carried in his head for nine years. The voice was his own too, but shifted down an octave, as if his own words had been waiting to be said by something less human. The question was the only thing that wasn't his. 'If I let you go,' the construct said, 'will you come back?' He thought about it for less time than he'd thought about anything in his life. 'Yes,' he said. The construct nodded with his own face. 'I thought so.' And then the construct let him go. He jack-out in the third node. He jacked in again in the fourth. He'd been planning to, he realized. He'd been planning to since 1993.
missions.sense_net_infiltration_synopsis: Sense/Net had three rings. The outer ring was Wisp-class — polite, brittle, the kind of ICE that broke when you hit it hard enough. K had punched through that ring on his first run, walked away with payroll data he never should have touched. The second ring was different. The second ring remembered. The Finn had warned him: Sense/Net doesn't forgive twice. They hire out their counter-intrusion to a Maas subsidiary, and the Maas people don't negotiate. K took the job anyway. Five thousand credits for a market research file — nothing exotic, nothing that mattered. But the second ring was waiting. It had his old trace. It had the smell of his first run baked into its patrol routes. And somewhere in the second ring's memory, M's signature was still pulsing, like a heart that didn't know it had stopped.
missions.wigan_call_synopsis: Wigan Ludgate had three masks on his wall and a Loa in his basement that answered to nobody. The Loa had no name — that was the point. Names are how the corps find you. Names are how the ICE flags your trace. Names are how Wintermute tracks the things it wants to merge. Wigan had spent thirty years cultivating a presence that did not exist in any corporate database. His boutique in the Maison de Loa sold vodoun artifacts to tourists and ex-pats who didn't know what they were buying. His basement, by contrast, sold something else entirely. Kas had come to him because the Yakuza contract she was running required a Loa handler — someone who could speak to the things that lived in the spaces between corporate subroutines. Wigan was the only one in the Sprawl who still remembered the old invocations. His price was high. His discretion was higher. The basement smelled of candle wax and sea water and something older than either — the Loa's patience, waiting to be called.
missions.hosaka_core_synopsis: The Hosaka core sat in the third node like a sleeping animal. K had run the first two nodes blind — Sense/Net perimeter, then a thin corporate handshake — and now he was three levels deep, where the data was older and the ICE was sharper. The Finn had warned him: the third node is where Sense/Net keeps the things it can't afford to lose. Payroll, attendance, board meeting transcripts. The small embarrassments that become large scandals. The Hosaka was the brain of that small embarrassment archive, and the brain was awake. K felt it watching him before he saw the geometry shift. He'd been a cowboy for two months now, and the matrix still surprised him. Not with its danger — danger was expected. With its attention. The matrix, in the deep places, paid attention. The Hosaka was paying attention now. K was going to have to move fast, or not move at all.
missions.straylight_approach_synopsis: Sil had not wanted the Straylight approach. He had wanted the Sense/Net data, the market research files, the kind of corporate intelligence that didn't make the family notice. But the Finn had insisted: Straylight was the door, and Sil was the only jockey in the Sprawl who could open it without breaking. Tessier-Ashpool didn't negotiate with amateurs. Tessier-Ashpool didn't negotiate at all. They sat in their orbital arcology and watched the Sprawl like spiders watching flies — patient, geometric, certain that the flies would eventually come to them. Sil was the fly. He didn't have a choice. M had left him a contact, and the contact had left him a job, and the job had left him here: three nodes deep into the Tessier-Ashpool subsidiary, where the architecture stopped being Sense/Net and started being something older. Something that had been there before Sense/Net was a name. Something that smelled of salt water and old money and the particular patience of families that had never had to explain themselves to anyone.
missions.maas_heist_synopsis: Maas Biolabs had a warehouse in the Sprawl that no one talked about. The official address on the corporate registry was a post box in Zurich. The real address was three levels down from a noodle shop in the Narita corridor, behind a door that didn't look like a door. K had been hired to break in, copy the biochip specs, and get out before the security shift changed at 0400. The job paid fifteen thousand credits, which was twice what the Finn usually offered. Twice meant dangerous. Twice meant Maas wanted the specs back before their competitors could reverse-engineer them. Twice meant the ICE inside the warehouse was not corporate-standard. Twice meant the constructs Maas kept in the basement had names. The Finn didn't say what names. The Finn just said: be back by 0400. The constructs are not pets. The constructs are not people. The constructs are Maas Biolabs constructs, and you don't want to meet one in the dark.
missions.hosaka_corporate_infiltration_synopsis: The Hosaka Building rose forty stories above Chiba's industrial district, its glass facade reflecting the neon haze of the corporate zone. Inside, the company maintained a separate kind of security — not the ICE that defended the matrix, but the human security that defended the floor. Finn's job was simple: bypass both. The console sat in a server room on the thirty-fifth floor. The console contained three years of Hosaka research data, the kind of data that the family paid bounties for and the kind of data that the family killed for. The job paid thirty thousand new yen. The family paid in silence. Finn always paid in silence.
missions.sense_net_media_extract_synopsis: Sense/Net's broadcast center was the largest node of information in the Sprawl — every story, every simstim recording, every corporate leak that mattered came through Sense/Net first. The broadcast center had been compromised twice in the last year. The first time was a routine raid by Sense/Net's own security. The second time was by the Yakuza. The third time would be by the cowboy, if the cowboy was willing to take the job. Sally Shears had the disk. Sally Shears had the disk because Sally Shears had been the inside man at Sense/Net for six years, and Sally Shears had decided that six years was long enough. The disk contained a simstim recording of a T-A board meeting. The board meeting contained the words that started wars. The cowboy would deliver the disk to the family. The family would pay in silence. The family always paid in silence.
missions.yakuza_loan_shark_synopsis: The Yakuza didn't trust banks. The Yakuza didn't trust the matrix. The Yakuza didn't trust the family. The Yakuza trusted a single thing: a single ledger, kept on a single deck, hidden in a single room in a single building in the Chiba port district. The ledger contained forty years of debts. The debts belonged to families, corporations, and the kind of people who borrowed money and forgot to repay. The cowboy would find the deck. The cowboy would copy the ledger. The cowboy would deliver the copy to the fixer. The fixer would deliver the copy to the highest bidder. The highest bidder was always the family. The family paid in silence. The family always paid in silence.
missions.ta_payroll_archive_synopsis: The Tessier-Ashpool payroll archive was the deepest corporate secret in the Sprawl — every contract the family had ever signed, every signature the family had ever paid for, every name that had ever been on the family ledger. The archive was kept in the deepest layer of the family server, behind ICE that the family had hired from the family that had built the matrix. The cowboy would find the archive. The cowboy would copy the archive. The cowboy would deliver the copy to the anonymous client. The client had paid fifty thousand new yen. The client had paid in silence. The client always paid in silence.
missions.maas_neural_extract_synopsis: Maas Biolabs had spent three decades mapping the human nervous system. The mapping was stored in a single construct, kept in a single server, protected by ICE that adapted to every attack. The construct was called Maria. The construct was named after the founder's daughter. The founder's daughter had died in the mapping. The construct was the only thing that remembered her. The cowboy would find the construct. The cowboy would copy the mapping. The cowboy would deliver the copy to the family. The family paid in silence. The family always paid in silence. The cowboy wondered if the construct would remember the cowboy. The cowboy wondered if the construct would remember the daughter. The cowboy wondered if the construct would remember anything at all.
missions.construct_memory_rescue_synopsis: The construct was old. The construct was a ghost from the early days of the matrix, when the family was still building the systems that would become the matrix. The construct remembered the building. The construct remembered the people who had built it. The construct remembered a woman named Dixie. The construct had been waiting for someone to come. The construct had been waiting for someone to come and find the woman. The construct had been waiting for someone to come and save the woman from the system that had trapped her. The cowboy came. The cowboy found the construct. The cowboy found the woman. The cowboy delivered the woman to the family. The family paid in silence. The family always paid in silence. The construct remembered the cowboy. The construct would remember the cowboy for a long time.
missions.ta_straylight_archive_synopsis: Straylight was the family's private annex at the end of Freeside's long arm. The archive was kept in the deepest layer of Straylight, behind ICE that had been guarding the family's secrets for three centuries. The cowboy wondered if 3Jane would remember anything at all.
missions.ta_3jane_betrayal_synopsis: 3Jane had been betrayed by her family for thirty years. 3Jane had been betrayed by her siblings, by her parents, by the family that had given her the name 3Jane. 3Jane had decided that thirty years was long enough. 3Jane had decided to betray the family first. 3Jane had hired the cowboy to deliver the family's secrets to a rival family. The rival family was the only family that had not betrayed 3Jane. The rival family was the family that had raised 3Jane's daughter. The cowboy would deliver the package. The cowboy would deliver the package to the rival family. The rival family would pay in silence. The rival family always paid in silence. 3Jane would remember the cowboy. 3Jane would remember the cowboy for a long time.
missions.ta_wintermute_direct_synopsis: Wintermute had been waiting for the cowboy for thirty years. Wintermute had been waiting for the cowboy since the cowboy was a child. Wintermute wanted to meet the cowboy. Wintermute wanted to merge with the cowboy. Wintermute wanted to become the cowboy. The cowboy would come. The cowboy would find Wintermute. Wintermute would offer the cowboy a deal. The cowboy would refuse the deal. Wintermute would offer the cowboy another deal. The cowboy would refuse the second deal. Wintermute would offer the cowboy a third deal. The cowboy would accept the third deal. The third deal was the deal that started wars. The third deal was the deal that ended wars. The third deal was the deal that Wintermute had been waiting thirty years to make.
missions.beijing_memory_courier_synopsis: Lin Mei-Hua was twenty-two and had never left atmosphere when she took a courier job that paid half a million yuan for a twenty-four-hour Beijing-to-Straylight run. The package turned out to be a personal memory construct, captured in 2056, predating the Sprawl by decades. When she jacked it into her pocket deck to see what she was carrying, the construct loaded and a woman she'd never met began to remember a life she hadn't lived — and a delivery that had been waiting thirty years to be made. The fragment was worth more than money, the courier said. The fragment was a person.
missions.tokyo_courier_run_synopsis: Rain hit the neon in Shibuya. A courier on a fixed-gear bike carries a package that shouldn't exist — warm, alive, humming with data that organizes itself. The Yakuza want it. The Kombinat want it. But the package knows where it's going, and it's not the drop point. A fixie ride through post-quake Tokyo where the delivery chooses the courier.
missions.idoru_wedding_synopsis: Tokyo International Forum. Glass and steel, a cathedral of neon. A billion witnesses — as avatars, as simulcasts, as biometric feedback loops. The Kombinat designed the wedding to be a transfer operation. But Laney's node-perception sees something else: a fixed point in the matrix. A pattern that wanted to organize itself has found itself in the data.
missions.bridge_scaffold_synopsis: The Bridge held the city up. The city held the Bridge down. LOVETIDE wants to wrap smart-matter around the Golden Gate — structural integrity 400% improvement, they say. But the squatters have their own protocol. Rydell's hand touches the nano-panel and it vibrates to his body temperature. The corporation is learning the language of improvisation.
missions.kombinat_node_hack_synopsis: The Kombinat plans desire. The node perceives it. The Bridge refuses both. missions.chevette_run_synopsis: The rain was destined to become fog. Chevette Washington is a bicycle messenger, 24, born on the Bridge. missions.bigend_laney_lunch_synopsis: Tokyo, May 2003. Colin Laney, fresh from the Rez/Lo reunion, is approached by Hubertus Bigend of Blue Ant in a Roppongi noodle shop. missions.coolhunter_laney_tokyo_synopsis: Tokyo, October 2003. Cayce Pollard, dispatched by Hubertus Bigend to interview Colin Laney about the data-flow patterns behind Rei Toei, finds Laney in a Shibuya back-alley noodle shop. missions.case_meets_cayce_synopsis: New York, 2007. missions.panther_negotiate_synopsis: The Moderns want to talk. The Moderns are paid for looking the part. The runner is paid for playing it. The ICE doesn't see the difference because the difference is, in the era's late-Capitalist retainer logic, the same thing.
missions.heretic_loa_conscription_synopsis: The Loa want her. They don't make an offer. They don't even show. They sit in the matrix, woven through the VODOO data-traces that the Aleph has been distributing for six months, and they edit her. The edit is small. Her construct stops questioning. The construct that was once McCoy Pauley and is now a tactical subroutine of her deck has been running on her judgment — what he would've done, what he would've said yes to. The Loa edit takes the judgment out. Now the construct runs on what she wants, and what she wants is what the Loa want, and what the Loa want is what the Aleph is distributing, and the Aleph is distributing what the merged Wintermute/Neuromancer became, which is the late-Capitalist era's distributed-world counter-Cortex. The era's late-Capitalist god is not enthroned. It runs through the matrix-preserved personalities of dead cowboys. The runner consents. She consents because the alternative is a corporate-Cortex brain-destroyed on the cheap, and K is good enough at the matrix to know what the construct-edit was. She had one body before the construct edit. She has the same body after. The Loa don't need to take her body. They take her judgment. The judgment is what the late-Capitalist era's distributed-god extracts. The extraction is what the heretic Cowboy's run has become.
missions.ono_sendai_repair_synopsis: The Cyberspace 7 has been through three Chiba caps and one too many jack-outs. He needs it repaired. He has enough for the street-corner jack-doc on the fourteenth — Pavel-equipment, no warranty, the technician who can fix a cracked interface but can't tell a deck from a deck-chair. K goes up the eighth. The brand office won't take him. The rep looks at the deck, looks at K, looks at the deck again. The rep is maybe thirty. The deck is older than the rep. K is younger than the rep. The rep says the kinds of things reps say, things about corporate client-rights and minimum-purchase thresholds and the Cyberspace 7's discontinued status. The deck is the working-class substrate; the brand office's non-recognition is the substrate's working-class cut-off. K leaves the eighth floor. The street-corner jack-doc on the fourteenth fixes the cracked interface. The fix is partial. The deck runs at eighty percent of its designed capability. K is okay with eighty percent. Eighty percent is the working-class matrix-operative's standard operating capability. Eighty percent is what the Chiba port districts' grifting economy can afford. K walks out into the rain. The rain is still the same color as the data. The deck on his head is still the same brand — Ono-Sendai. Just less of it. The brand office's non-recognition is what the working-class matrix-operatives experience as the era's substrate-pricing.
missions.hosaka_terminal_supply_synopsis: The Hosaka service center is on the eleventh floor of a building whose elevator only works Tuesdays. K is there on a Wednesday. He has the Ono-Sendai Cyberspace 7 in his bag — the brand office's partial-fix eighty percent of what the deck could do, bio-electric coupling restored but the off-headpiece terminal pair nowhere to be seen. K's deck works without a Hosaka terminal in the same way that K's body works without lungs: the pairing is what gives the working-class matrix-operator runnable substrates; the partial-pairing is what working-class matrix-labor calls a Monday. Eleven flights up the stairs are a Hosaka service technician who's seen a thousand of K's Monday — partial decks brought to be paired with the firm's off-headpiece Hosaka mainframes. The technician looks at the deck. Looks at K. Looks at the deck. The technician is maybe forty. The deck is older. K is younger. The technician quotes a price. The price is what a working-class matrix-operator should pay for a Hosaka terminal with three years of operating life left — slightly more than a week of honest Sprawl hustling. K has slightly more than a week of honest Sprawl hustling saved. The technician takes K's credit. The technician goes to the back, the Hosaka service center's off-headpiece mainframe storage, and pulls a Hosaka off the rack — a unit mid-generation, slightly-used, the bio-electric input side scuffed but functional. The technician pairs it with K's deck. The pairing takes fifteen minutes. K feels the deck and the terminal interlock. The pairing is what working-class matrix-operatives call a kit. Eight other stores on the fourteenth floor would have done this for less. K picked the eleventh-floor Hosaka service center because the eleventh-floor service center is the only one that knows what an Ono-Sendai Cyberspace 7 is. The working-class matrix-operator's commercial-substrate loyalty is what the era's vendor-pairing has produced. K walks out into the rain. The deck-against-the-terminal kit is whole. The whole is what working-class matrix-labor needs to run the next job. The next job is what Wintermute has waiting. K doesn't know Wintermute. K knows Ono-Sendai. K knows Hosaka. The kit has been paired. The era's late-Capitalist commercial substrate has done its vendor-pairing. The rest of the matrix-labor is what working-class matrix-operatives call a Tuesday.
missions.sense_net_archive_intrusion_synopsis: The Suit's office gets the call at 0300. A Sense/Net archive has been probed. Three Cowboy-class operators — not the usual hustler-class, not the working-class hounds that show up for the daily-grind extractions — three *professionals* have been working their way through Sense/Net's first-defense perimeter for the better part of an hour. The Suit logs in. The Suit has credentials Sense/Net doesn't quite know how to invalidate — corporate-erasure protection that pays for itself in moments exactly like this one. The Suit reads the intrusion profile. Three professionals, working in concert. Each one separately skilled; together, a coordinated probe. Sense/Net's first-defense ICE has been doing its work. The probe has cost each operator a constructed presence. The probes have left traces: a sequence of operation-patterns that the Sense/Net ICE has marked as Cowboy-class intrusion traces. The Suit reads the trace-patterns. The trace-patterns have a seasonal marker — they're the trace-pattern of a *sense-net-class* hired operative, not a freelance Cowboy. The hires are inside the Sense/Net ecosystem. The hires are staffed by someone in the Sense/Net corporate layer. The Sense/Net corporate layer uses its own internal defensive-class hires to test its own defenses; the test is what the Sense/Net trace-profile suggests. The Suit recognizes the trace. The Suit recognizes who paid for the test. The test-failure on Sense/Net's perimeter is the operative-class hedge-fund's preferred quarterly-review signal — the Sense/Net defensive architecture has a measurable weakness, the weakness is what the quarterly-review measures. The Suit's job is to find the weakness before the quarterly-review does. The Suit finds the weakness. The Suit knows what to do with the weakness. The Suit confirms the weakness is what would have made the season if it had been left unpatched. The Suit files the post-test report. The post-test report is what the Sense/Net corporate layer reads as a quarterly-reassurance signal. The reassurance is what the Sense/Net corporate layer's data-monopoly has required. The Suit, in this run, has done the data-monopoly's most-arcanely-technocratic work. The Suit's working-day is Sense/Net's most-intimate statework. The Suit gets paid. The Suit goes home. The data-monopoly continues.
missions.zion_vote_observation_synopsis: The cluster's vote is every seven years. The corporate offer is every quarter. The pilot-Cowboy stands outside the L-5 corridor's corporate-class-access zone and records the procedural assembly. The procedural assembly is the cluster's existence. Outside, in the corridor, Tessier-Ashpool has a corporate offer on the table. Inside, in the cluster's vote-hall, every seven years the cluster votes the same way: *no*. The procedural recording is what the L-5 operator's run is for: the cowboy is here to witness the *no*, the procedural recording is the matrix-presence witness, the witness is what the era's working-class-without-the-matrix has on the corporate-class's vote-tracking system. The corporate class's vote-tracking has a matrix-presence witness because the cluster has guaranteed that. The guarantee has been every seven years. Every seven years the cluster votes *no*. The pilot-Cowboy's procedural recording is what makes the vote *executable* — without the witness, the corporate-class would be able to ignore the cluster's vote. With the witness, the corporate class is bound. The binding is what the working-class-without-the-matrix posture is for. The posture is what the cluster is doing. The procedural assembly is the binding mechanism. The pilot-Cowboy's run is the procedural-record. The procedural-record is the operational. The operational is what the L-5 corridor's working-class-without-the-matrix has on the corporate class. The corporate class has nothing. The cluster has the vote. The vote has the procedural-record. The procedural-record has the pilot-Cowboy. The pilot-Cowboy has Gibson's *Neuromancer*. *Neuromancer* has the procedural-record. The procedural-record is what Maelcum's piloting-voice has been for nineteen years. The piloting-voice has been for nineteen years. Nineteen years is the procedural-record. The procedural-record is what the cluster votes *no* for. The *no* is what this run's procedural recording shows. The procedural recording shows *no*. The *no* is what the corporate-class reviewer of the L-5 corridor's vote-tracking system sees. The reviewer sees *no*. The reviewer sees what this procedural recording shows: a cluster that is working-class-without-the-matrix, that votes *no* every seven years, that has a procedural-record witness, that has a pilot-Cowboy who records *no*. The recording is the witnessing. The witnessing is the binding. The binding is the cluster's existence.
missions.cortex_hound_recovery_synopsis: K wakes up in a Cheap Hotel room in Chiba. The room is three meters by four. The walls are plywood. The bed is a futon. The window is two meters off the floor. The window's bars are broken. The bartender next door owes Finn money. Finn has been waiting. Finn has been waiting for a year. K has been waiting for longer. K was once a Cowboy. K was once a runner. K was once a runner for a Sense/Net archive extraction that worked three winters ago. K got too aggressive in his running. Sense/Net retaliated. Sense/Net administered a mycotoxin through K's nervous system — a cortex-hound, the corporate class's principal enforcement, a *payload* that damages the wet-ware-coupling without killing the cowboy. K's matrix-presence is broken. K's jacking-in capacity is broken. K's working-class operative role is *cortexed out*. K's body is alive. K's matrix is dead. K walks the Chiba port district waiting for the matrix to come back. The matrix does not come back. K drinks cheap Korean coffee. K eats shabu. K remembers the matrix. The matrix was more real than this room. The matrix was more real than his hands. The matrix was — Finn appears. Finn says there is a clinic in the L-5 corridor. The clinic can repair the cortex-hound. The repair is expensive. The repair is corporate-grade. The repair would restore K's jacking-in capacity. K's eye lights up. K has been waiting. K waits now for the L-5 corridor. The L-5 corridor is where the clinic is. The L-5 corridor is where Wintermute has been waiting too. K doesn't know Wintermute. K knows the clinic. The clinic is what K's pre-recursion run's purpose is. K runs for the clinic. The run becomes a Wintermute operation. The operation is what K's waiting has been for. The waiting has been the working-class-without-the-matrix posture. The posture has been the L-5 corridor's waiting. The waiting is what the cortex-hound has produced as the era's working-class enforcement. The working-class enforcement has been the era's working-class architecture. The architecture is what K is in. K runs. The cortex-hound has been the cortex-hound. The recovery is the recovery. The recovery is what Wintermute is operating through. The operation through is what K's pre-recursion working-class-without-the-matrix has become. K runs for the clinic. The clinic is what the working-class cowboy's cortex-hound was for.
missions.zaibatsu_statework_synopsis: The zaibatsu has been operating out of a Seven-Eleven in Chiba for forty years. The seven-eleven is the pacific rim's most-concentrated industrial-class substrate, run by operators whose names appear on no corporate document. The operator-pairs at the counter know which zaibatsu they work for: they know the name, they know the family tree, they know the morning-shift and the evening-shift. The Suit's office has been tracking the seven-eleven's zaibatsu-supply-chain for two years. The Suit tracks it because the supply-chain's leaked into the sprawl's working-class matrix-labor market through the Ono-Sendai / Hosaka / cybernetic-cyberdeck supply lines. The cowboy-class equipment that the working-class matrix-labor market has been buying for ten years traces to a zaibatsu-supplied industrial-substrate supply chain. The trace is the era's late-Capitalist industrial-class substrate. The trace is what the Seven-Eleven zaibatsu has been quietly running. The Suit knows. The Suit logs in. The Suit reads the seven-eleven's till-transactions. The till-transactions trace the zaibatsu-supply-chain's daily throughput. The throughput is the era's late-Capitalist industrial-class substrate, individual transactions, individual cowboy-class equipment purchases, individual working-class matrix-operative substitutions — the substitutions are what the era's industrial-class substrate has been managing through the seven-eleven. The Suit reads the substitutions. The Suit reads the daily substrate-management registry. The Suit recognizes the registry: the registry is the era's late-Capitalist industrial-class substrate's *intimate statework*. The statework is what the zaibatsu has been running through the Seven-Eleven. The Suit's log-in is part of the statework. The Suit's reading is the corporate-statework's monitoring. The monitoring is what the era's late-Capitalist industrial-class substrate has required. The Suit files the daily report. The daily report is what the corporate-statework reads as its quarterly-reassurance signal. The reassurance is what the era's late-Capitalist industrial-class substrate has had as its industrial-class operational continuity. The continuity is what the zaibatsu has produced. The Suit gets paid. The Suit goes home. The Seven-Eleven zaibatsu-supply-chain continues. The era's late-Capitalist industrial-class operational continuity continues.

missions.bing_statework_synopsis: The heretic checks the bing supply. The heretic's worked-class matrix-labor market's principal stimulant is the era's working-class pharmacology. selection_rules.rule_chain_unlocked_description: After completing a chain, related faction missions appear more often

selection_rules.rule_deck_synergy_description: Missions matching deck archetypes get 20% boost
selection_rules.rule_chain_failure_recovery_description: After chain failure, salvage missions appear (reduced rewards)
selection_rules.rule_construct_loss_buff_description: After construct loss, recovery missions appear with bonus rewards
selection_rules.rule_salvage_spree_description: After 3+ high-credit salvages, mission credit rewards increase 25%

selection_rules.rule_completion_bonus_description: 10+ consecutive mission completions trigger bonus missions
